name: Good sunglasses

lead: Sunglasses are tinted or polarized eyewear that cuts glare and ultraviolet exposure, and frame shape changes how the face reads. People pick frames to balance facial proportions, soften or hide features they dislike such as a weak eye area, and add polish, as a cheap alternative to surgery.

Tinted lenses cut visible light and UV, while the frame's shape, width, and bridge alter perceived proportions. The eye protection is supported by ophthalmic and dermatological guidance, and the American Optometric Association recommends UV-blocking sunglasses in sunlight. The face-shape advice is a style convention for which no controlled study was found.

paras: People try frame shapes and widths against their face shape, choosing bigger or more angular frames to balance features, and wear them daily outdoors and in photos. The visual effect shows the moment they are on.
Poorly rated lenses can let UV in, so guidance is to check for UV400 or equivalent labeling. Badly fitting frames are uncomfortable. The effect lasts only while worn.

angle.text: Users pick frame shapes to balance facial proportions and cover features they dislike, such as a weak eye area, as a cheap alternative to surgery. The change shows the moment they go on; glare protection is established, while the shape-to-face advice is style opinion.

lead: Sunglasses are tinted or darkened eyewear designed mainly to reduce glare and protect the eyes from bright light, including ultraviolet radiation, and they have been a fashion accessory since the 1920s and 1930s.[1] In appearance advice they are used in two ways: as a direct styling tool, where frame shape and width change how the face reads, and as a cover for the eye area, which looksmaxxing communities treat as a quick way to reduce the visibility of features they dislike.[2][3]

The protective function is supported by ophthalmic and dermatological guidance. The American Optometric Association is cited by Wikipedia as recommending UV-blocking sunglasses whenever a person is in sunlight, and photoprotection reviews list sunglasses among physical measures alongside hats, clothing and sunscreen.[1][4][5] UV exposure is described in a 2024 review as the main cause of photoageing, so protecting the eyes and the delicate skin around them is also an appearance habit with a long horizon.[5]

The cosmetic claims are mostly stylistic. Guides recommend particular shapes for particular face shapes, and a small body of psychology research has measured how faces are rated with and without sunglasses, with a Japanese study finding lower attractiveness and trust ratings for faces wearing sunglasses and a 2025 series of experiments finding that partly hidden faces can be rated as more attractive.[6][6]
infobox: UV400 (blocks about 99% or more of UVA and UVB up to 400 nm)[1]
Regulated by the FDA; ANSI Z80.3 transmittance categories[1]

paras: Frames are generally made of plastic, nylon, metal, metal alloys or wood. Nylon is common in sport because it is light and flexible, while metal frames are more rigid. Nose-bridge height is chosen to fit the wearer's nose, and lens colours such as grey and green are described as neutral because they preserve colour, with brown giving more contrast and yellow or amber used in low light.[1]

Lens materials include glass, which is clearest but heavy, acrylic, polycarbonate, which is lightest and most impact-resistant, and CR-39, the most common plastic. Further options are mirrored coatings, gradient lenses, photochromic lenses that darken in UV light, and polarised lenses that reduce glare from water and roads.[1]

Wikipedia lists well-known fashion shapes with their origins: the aviator, introduced by Bausch & Lomb in 1936 for US military pilots; the Ray-Ban Wayfarer, introduced in 1952 and the best-selling model from 1980 to 1999; the browline, adapted into sunglasses in the 1980s; wrap-arounds, derived from aviators in the 1960s; oversized frames; teashades; and shutter shades.[1]

Wikipedia traces precursors to Inuit snow goggles with narrow slits, used since about the thirteenth century, and to smoky quartz panes used in China in the twelfth century or earlier, with accounts that Chinese judges wore them to conceal expressions.[1] Eighteenth-century Venetians wore tinted 'gondola glasses', and Jean-Marie-Theodore Fieuzal (1836-1888) argued for UV protection with yellow-tinted glass. Rodenstock produced possibly the first sunglasses aimed at UV in 1899, and Crookes lenses containing cerium were introduced in 1913.[1]

Movie stars popularised sunglasses in the early 1920s. Sam Foster began selling inexpensive celluloid sunglasses under the Foster Grant name in Atlantic City in 1929. Edwin Land's Polaroid polarised lenses appeared in 1936, and Life magazine reported in 1938 that 20 million pairs had been sold in the US in 1937.[1]

Specific designs became tied to public figures: Wikipedia says aviators gained popularity through Douglas MacArthur in the 1940s and later through musicians such as Freddie Mercury, and that a 1982 product-placement deal put them in Top Gun. Wayfarers were worn by James Dean, Elvis Presley and Bob Marley, and teashades by 1960s counterculture figures including John Lennon.[1]

Tinted lenses lower visible-light transmission, and UV-filtering coatings or materials reduce ultraviolet exposure. Eye-protection guidance recommends lenses that filter 99% or more of UVA and UVB, often labelled UV400, and Wikipedia says protection can only be confirmed by measuring the lenses, with standards allowing general classification.[1]

Wikipedia also notes that dark lenses without UV filtering can be more harmful than none because the pupil dilates and lets in more UV radiation, and that price does not guarantee protection, citing a survey in which a $6.95 pair outperformed a designer brand.[1] Frame fit matters for stray light: lenses should be close enough to the face that little light enters from the sides, without touching the eyelashes.[1]

ISO 12312 has three parts: general-use sunglasses (first published 2013, revised 2022), filters for directly viewing the sun (2015) and sports eyewear (2022). Australia introduced a national standard in 1971, and its current standard uses five ratings from 0 to 4. The European standard EN 1836:2005 uses categories 0 to 4, requires 95% blocking up to 380 nm, and has no UV400 rating. In the United States the FDA regulates sunglasses, and ANSI Z80.3 sets UVB and UVA transmittance limits.[1]

Wikipedia notes that sunglasses cannot protect against permanent damage from looking directly at the sun, even during an eclipse, and that the UK labels lenses below 8% light transmission as unsuitable for driving.[1]

Style guidance generally pairs frame shape with face shape. A looksmax.org guide recommends wayfarers, rectangular frames or flat-top aviators for long or oblong faces to reduce apparent verticality and add width, boxy or angular frames for round faces to add angles, and round or oval frames for square faces to soften the jaw.[3] The guide warns that narrow frames are said to make a head look longer.[3]
These recommendations are style conventions and have not been tested in controlled studies.

subs.h: Hiding and reframing the eye area
paras: Looksmaxxing posts describe sunglasses as covering features such as canthal tilt, orbital bones, rounder eyes or a long midface, and as adding mystery.[2][3][7] Wikipedia notes sunglasses hide eye contact and emotions, which can be seen as desirable or intimidating, and that many professional poker players wear them for this reason.[1] The same source mentions the German entertainer Heino, whose trademark look is linked to bulging eyes.[1]

subs.h: Research on how sunglass-wearers are seen
paras: A study by Takehara and colleagues, indexed in PubMed as published in Discover Psychology in 2023, asked Japanese participants to rate faces with no covering, masks, sunglasses, or both at two time points in 2020 and 2022. Unoccluded faces received the highest ratings on social traits, sunglasses had a significant negative effect, and faces wearing both lowest.[6]

A 2025 paper in Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications examined the 'less is more' effect, in which partly hidden faces are rated more attractive; across three experiments it reported the effect was stronger after the pandemic began, stronger for unfamiliar faces, and stronger for faces of initially low attractiveness, and one experiment concerned sunglasses specifically.[6] A 2026 eye-tracking study found sunglasses reduced and delayed viewers' looks to the speaker during conversations.[6] Findings across these studies are mixed and measure ratings of photographed faces rather than real encounters.

Photoprotection reviews list sunglasses among physical measures, alongside clothing, hats and sunscreen, against ultraviolet exposure.[4][5] UV radiation is described in a 2024 review as the main cause of photoageing, photoimmunosuppression and photocarcinogenesis.[5] Sunglasses protect the eyes and the skin around them, though most of the cited evidence addresses sun protection in general rather than eyewear alone.

Wikipedia lists photokeratitis, cataracts, pterygium and eye cancers as possible consequences of excessive UV exposure, and notes that high-energy visible (blue) light has been linked to age-related macular degeneration, although the evidence is debated.[1]

Sunglasses can improve driving safety by reducing glare but may be too dark for driving if poorly chosen, and photochromic lenses react slowly behind car windscreens that filter UV.[1] Polarised lenses can interfere with aircraft windscreens and some instrument displays.[1] Frames that fit poorly can be uncomfortable. Labelling varies by region.[1]

In looksmax.org threads, sunglasses are discussed as a cheap alternative to eye-area procedures, with one thread titled around a crutch and a post comparing a pound-and-a-half pair of shades with the cost of orbital surgery.[2] Another thread claims sunglasses improve how people with long midfaces or round eyes look, and that people wearing shades indoors tend to look different without them.[7] Threads also ask which frames suit a long midface, whether to wear sunglasses all the time, and which UV-protecting pairs to buy.[8][9]

The terms used in these posts, including 'fraud', 'PSL boost' and 'looksmin', are community slang: fraud here means disguising a trait, PSL is the forum rating scale, and looksmin means something that lowers apparent looks.

Reference descriptions list features to compare: a UV400 or equivalent standard label, lens tint and polarisation, frame material, nose-bridge fit, and snug fit to the face to limit stray light.[1] The same source says protection can only be confirmed by measuring lenses, so labels indicating conformity with a named standard are the usual indicator.[1] Luxottica and Safilo produce most major brands, according to Wikipedia, with revenue of about 9 billion euros and 1 billion euros in 2018 respectively.[1]

No studies found that test sunglasses for real-world facial attractiveness. Related research includes a Turkish survey of 17,769 university students in which 60% reported using sunglasses, behind sunscreen at 64%,[10] a randomised trial of sunglasses for conjunctival symptoms of seasonal rhinitis,[11] and perception studies on faces with sunglasses noted above.[6][6] A 2026 randomised trial in the Journal of Affective Disorders tested blue-blocking glasses for mania, which concerns a different kind of eyewear and condition.[12]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sunglasses are discussed as a cheap accessory that hides or reframes the eye area and midface, rather than mainly for eye protection. [2][3][7]

claims.claim: Sunglasses are a cheap substitute for eye-area surgery and hide flaws such as bad canthal tilt or recessed orbitals.
Specific frame shapes balance facial proportions depending on face shape.
